Kidneys and Fat
KID-neez and FAT
noun
Kidney is of uncertain Middle English origin; fat is from Old English fætt, well-fed, rich. Together they render the Hebrew kelayoth (kidneys, seat of the affections) and heleb (the choice fat), the inward portions reserved as the LORD’s.

Biblical Definition

The two kidneys and the fat upon them were, by the law of the offerings, the LORD’s special portion, taken away and burnt upon the altar: “the two kidneys, and the fat that is on them, which is by the flanks” (Lev 3:4, 3:10). The fat was reckoned the best and richest of the beast, and the LORD claimed it as His own — “all the fat is the LORD’S” (Lev 3:16). The kidneys, deep-seated and hidden, were in Hebrew thought the seat of the affections and the secret reins that God alone tries and knows. So the very parts offered spoke of the innermost man. The prophets take up the figure in judgment and in blessing: the sword of the LORD is made fat “with the fat of the kidneys of rams” (Isa 34:6), and Israel was fed with “the fat of kidneys of wheat” (Deu 32:14), the choicest of the harvest. That the fat is the LORD’S teaches a great and abiding truth: God is worthy of the best and will not be put off with the lean and the leftover. To give Him the fat is to own that the richest of our substance, and the secret affections of our reins, belong wholly to Him. He who tries the reins asks the heart’s best; and He gave His own best, His only-begotten, that we might learn to withhold nothing.

Webster 1828 Definition

The two kidneys and the choice fat upon them, reserved as the LORD’s portion in the offerings.

expand to see more

KIDNEYS AND FAT, the inward organs and the rich fat about them, burnt upon the altar as the LORD’s portion.

The fat was accounted the best of the beast, and the law declared that all the fat is the LORD’s.

The kidneys were held to be the seat of the secret affections, the reins that God tries.

The prophets use the fat of kidneys as a figure of the choicest of a thing, whether of rams or of wheat.

The word fat is from Old English fætt, meaning rich or well-fed.

Key Scripture

Lev 3:4 — "And the two kidneys, and the fat that is on them, which is by the flanks, and the caul above the liver, with the kidneys, it shall he take away."

Lev 3:10 — "And the two kidneys, and the fat that is upon them, which is by the flanks, and the caul above the liver, with the kidneys, it shall he take away."

Isa 34:6 — "The sword of the LORD is filled with blood, it is made fat with fatness, and with the blood of lambs and goats, with the fat of the kidneys of rams: for the LORD hath a sacrifice in Bozrah, and a great slaughter in the land of Idumea."

Deu 32:14 — "Butter of kine, and milk of sheep, with fat of lambs, and rams of the breed of Bashan, and goats, with the fat of kidneys of wheat; and thou didst drink the pure blood of the grape."

Modern Corruption

A portion of the offering, not a contested doctrine; it recovers that the best and the inmost belong to the LORD.

expand to see more

The kidneys and the fat rebuke the man who brings God the lean and keeps the fat for himself. The age offers its leftovers to heaven and lavishes its richest upon its own pleasure; it gives God the thin edges of its time and treasure. But the law that burnt the fat upon the altar declares that the best is His by right, and that to withhold it is to rob Him of His portion.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that the fat is the LORD’s. He is worthy of the choicest, and He tries the reins and the hidden affections. To give Him the fat and the kidneys is to yield Him both the richest of our substance and the secret of our hearts, withholding nothing from the God who withheld not His own Son.

Usage

"The fat is the LORD’s; He will not be served with the lean and the leftover."

"He who tries the reins asks for the heart’s best, not its remnants."

"As the fat of kidneys was the choicest of the beast, so God claims the choicest of us."
